name: ViEWS (Violence Early-Warning System) and the 2023/24 VIEWS Prediction Challenge. Core paper: Hegre, Vesco, Colaresi et al. (2025), 'The 2023/24 VIEWS Prediction challenge: Predicting the number of fatalities in armed conflict, with uncertainty', Journal of Peace Research 62(6):2070-2087. System context: Hegre et al. (2019) 'ViEWS: A political Violence Early-Warning System' (JPR 56(2)) and Hegre et al. (2021) 'ViEWS2020: Revising and evaluating the ViEWS political Violence Early-Warning System' (JPR 58(3):599-611). Predecessor: Hegre, Vesco & Colaresi (2022) and Vesco et al. (2022), the escalation prediction competition (International Interactions 48(4)).
type: paper + benchmark/challenge protocol (method family: pre-registered, multi-team prospective forecasting challenge with fixed proper scoring rules, public benchmarks and a true-future window), with an open evaluation repository
url: https://doi.org/10.1177/00223433241300862 (open-access PDF, CC BY: https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/226622/1/hegre-et-al-2025-the-2023-24-views-prediction-challenge-predicting-the-number-of-fatalities-in-armed-conflict-with.pdf) ; preprint (pre-analysis-plan function, 8 Jul 2024): https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.11045 ; online appendix: https://viewsforecasting.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/OnlineAppendix_PredictionChallenge_2023-1.pdf ; original invitation v1.2 (Apr 2023): https://viewsforecasting.org/wp-content/uploads/VIEWS_2023.24_Prediction_Competition_Invitation.pdf ; leaderboard: https://viewsforecasting.org/leaderboard/ ; dashboard: https://predcomp.viewsforecasting.org ; evaluation and benchmark code: https://github.com/prio-data/prediction_competition_2023 ; ViEWS2020: https://doi.org/10.1177/0022343320962157
year: 2025 (JPR online 6 May 2025, vol. 62 issue 6). Preprint July 2024. Invitation April 2023. True-future window 1 Jul 2024 to 30 Jun 2025. The live leaderboard was last updated around Dec 2025 [uncertain]. The promised separate evaluation article (planned for fall 2025) was not found as of 2026-10-17.
authors: Havard Hegre, Paola Vesco, Michael Colaresi, Jonas Vestby and about 37 co-authors from the 13 contributing teams (PRIO, Uppsala, KIT, CCEW Munich, Trinity College Dublin, UT Dallas, UCL, Essex, Turin, CSIC Barcelona, Georgia Tech, West Virginia, among others). Scoring committee: Philip Schrodt, Celine Cunen, Thomas Mayer (PREVIEW, German Foreign Office), Seth Caldwell (formerly UN OCHA). Funded by the German Foreign Office, ERC (ANTICIPATE, 101055176) and the Research Council of Norway.
popularity: As of 2026-10-17: Crossref 7 citations, Semantic Scholar 10 citations. GitHub prio-data/prediction_competition_2023: 7 stars, 7 forks, no license file, last push 2025-12-08. 24 contributions from 13 teams. The parent ViEWS system papers (2019, 2021) are widely cited in conflict forecasting, and ViEWS forecasts appear in UN and government dashboards.
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (Journal of Peace Research, 2025; ViEWS 2019/2021 also JPR). The individual team write-ups are working papers or self-reported. The leaderboard is a live web page, not peer-reviewed.
target_type: Count target (monthly number of state-based conflict fatalities), forecast as a full predictive distribution (15 to 1,000 samples per unit-month). It is neither a pure onset target nor a state target. Because counts persist strongly (the 'conflict trap'), the task rewards persistence in much the same way a state target does: most of the score comes from ongoing wars, and the hardest cases are outbreaks in previously peaceful units. Earlier ViEWS (2019/2020) used binary targets: P(at least 25 battle-related deaths) per country-month, and later P(at least 1 BRD) at both levels.
target_definition: y = UCDP 'best' estimate of state-based conflict fatalities in unit i in month t, on the raw (non-logged) count scale. The predecessor competition used ln(y+1) change. Horizons: true future July 2024 (s=3) to June 2025 (s=14), from data up to and including April 2024. The 2-month gap reflects the release lag of UCDP Candidate data. Retrospective test windows: each month of calendar years 2018 to 2023, from data up to October of the preceding year (s=3..14). Contributors could submit identical predictions for all 12 months or fine-tune each step. ViEWS2020 trains a separate model for each step s = 1..36 months.
spatial_unit: country-month (cm, global, Gleditsch-Ward country list with CShapes borders) and PRIO-GRID-month (pgm, 0.5 x 0.5 degree cells, about 55 x 55 km at the equator; Africa and the Middle East only).
at_risk_masking: None. Every unit-month is scored, including units already in ongoing war, and there is no onset/at-risk mask. Most of each score therefore comes from continuing conflicts: 9 of the 10 largest CRPS values for the exactly-zero benchmark were Ethiopia and Ukraine. This is the reason persistence-type benchmarks are so strong. The contrast with our design is that D-020 plus the onset mask (rows already under alert are excluded) deliberately removes this persistence credit. ViEWS results are therefore not directly comparable to an onset metric.
data_sources: UCDP Georeferenced Event Dataset (GED, final, vetted) for the retrospective test windows 2018 to 2023. UCDP Candidate Events Dataset (monthly preliminary release) for 2024 onward and for scoring the true future. The VIEWS team supplied about 100 features at each level: training data 1990 to 2017, prediction inputs for the test windows, and updated data up to April 2024 (released June 2024). Contributors could add their own data, for example a corpus of 6 million news articles (ConflictForecast LDA topics) and actor/dyad data (HCD_dyad).
data_source_variant: Two label versions are mixed across windows. The test windows are scored against final UCDP-GED, and the true future against UCDP-Candidate. ViEWS2020 itself notes that Candidate data are vetted less carefully than GED, so 'some systematic differences between the two periods may be reflected in the evaluation'. It also reports a Candidate reporting error that was later corrected. This is the analogue of our official-file vs alerts.in.ua split (D-007/D-015): a label-source change between the development windows and the prospective window.
preprocessing: VIEWS aggregates UCDP events to cm and pgm. Assignment rules differ between levels: a pgm cell spanning several countries aggregates all its events, while cm assigns events to the country where they happened, so the two levels are not fully compatible. A country enters cm only for the months it exists in the Gleditsch-Ward list. Submissions were standardised to 1,000 samples: point predictions were converted to Poisson(mean = variance = prediction), and odd sample counts were up-sampled with scipy.signal.resample. The int32 sample format was fixed in advance.
known_label_artefacts: (1) Preliminary vs final labels: the true future is scored on UCDP Candidate data, which UCDP later revises into GED, so the scores may change after the vetted release [uncertain whether a rescoring on final GED is planned]. (2) Extreme zero inflation: 87% of cm and 99% of pgm observations are zero, which makes 'exactly zero' a hard benchmark at pgm. (3) Heavy right tail: rare huge counts (Ethiopia 2021-22, Ukraine 2022) dominate mean CRPS and MIS. The organisers mitigated this by averaging six test years and adding the ab-Log score, which uses bins so that far-away mass does not dominate. (4) Cross-level aggregation mismatch (cm vs pgm). (5) A Candidate-data reporting error in ViEWS2020 was kept until the vetted data replaced it. Duplicates, gaps and swapped columns are not discussed. The analogues for us are partial recording days and the 30-minute ends (D-010/D-013).
model_family: Benchmarks: exactly-zero; last-historical with Poisson noise; conflictology_country12 (the empirical distribution of the unit's last 12 monthly values); conflictology_neighbors12 (last 12 months in the cell plus first-order neighbours); conflictology_bootstrap240 (global draws from the last 20 years). Contributions: empirical-quantile and negative binomial history models (Drauz & Becker; Bodentien & Rueter); Bayesian Tweedie/NB/Poisson GLMM and GAM (Brandt); hurdle tree ensembles and AutoML (CCEW trees; D'Orazio); a three-stage hierarchical hurdle with Platt scaling (Fritz et al.); zero-inflated GAM and stacked ML (Muchlinski & Thornhill); observed, hidden and Gaussian-process Markov models (Randahl & Vegelius); random forest with news LDA topics (ConflictForecast); Dynamic Time Warping shape matching (PaCE; HCD_dyad); temporal fusion transformer (CCEW_tft); a pre-trained transformer with NB likelihood (UNITO). The ViEWS core system (2020) uses step-specific random forests and logits combined by EBMA ensembling.
features: Common VIEWS feature sets (about 100 per level): conflict history (lags and decay functions of fatalities by violence type), spatial lags and neighbourhood conflict, and structural covariates (demography, economy, V-Dem regime indicators, geography). Team additions: rolling 3/6/8-month averages and temporal lags (Muchlinski & Thornhill); 15 LDA news topics (ConflictForecast); actor-dyad clusters (HCD_dyad); time-invariant covariates and known future inputs (TFT). The strongest true-future entries rely mostly on the unit's own recent history: the 12-month empirical distribution, Markov states, and NB fits to recent history.
external_feature_timing: Inputs are frozen at the data cut-off (October of the previous year for test windows; April 2024 for the true future). Forecasts start at s=3, which covers the publication lag of the conflict data. For news topics and other external covariates the paper does not document publication lags or vintages [uncertain]. In the retrospective windows, whether each covariate was available in real time (a real-time vintage) rather than as a later revised value is not stated. Only the true-future window guarantees that inputs were real-time.
ablation_design: No formal ablation in the challenge paper. All models are scored on the same units, months and windows (like-for-like), which allows clean cross-model comparison. ViEWS2020 contains an ensemble 'drop-one' analysis: the change in ensemble AUPR when each constituent model is removed, with 'harm' defined as more than 0.5 bootstrapped standard errors. Some team papers compare variants internally, for example local vs global trees and NB vs hurdle vs neural network.
split_scheme: Challenge: (a) six retrospective calendar-year test windows 2018 to 2023, each forecast from data up to October of the prior year, all in the same s=3..14 format; (b) one true-future window, Jul 2024 to Jun 2025, from data up to April 2024, submitted by 23 June 2024 before any outcome existed. The scoring committee gives roughly equal weight to the test windows and the true future. The protocol changed mid-challenge. The April 2023 invitation planned a true future of calendar 2024 (data to October 2023), test windows 2018-2021, final forecasts due 10 Dec 2023, and an evaluation article in May 2025. The final protocol extended the test windows to 2023 and moved the true future to Jul 2024 to Jun 2025. ViEWS2020 core system: evaluation periodisation trains Jan 1990 to Dec 2012, calibrates and tunes on Jan 2013 to Dec 2015, and tests on Jan 2016 to Dec 2018. Forecast periodisation trains 1990 to Dec 2015, calibrates on Jan 2016 to Dec 2018, then RETRAINS on train+calibration and forecasts Jan 2020 to Dec 2022. Published monthly forecasts from Jul 2018 to Dec 2019 were later scored against actuals (retrospective evaluation of true forecasts).
metrics: Main: CRPS (properscoring/xskillscore crps_ensemble, equal sample weights, empirical CDF; for counts this is effectively the ranked probability score). Secondary I: adjusted binned log score (ab-Log). Bins are [0], [1-2], [3-5], [6-10], [11-25], [26-50], [51-100], [101-250], [251-500], [501-1000], [1001+], with one pseudo-sample (omega = 1) per bin, so the formula is -log((p*1000+1)/1011). The cap stops a zero-probability outcome giving an infinite score. Secondary II: Mean Interval Score at 90% (NumPy linear quantiles). 90% was chosen because quantiles of overdispersed distributions beyond it are unreliable with 1,000 samples. A candidate pseudo-Earth-Mover divergence was discussed in the invitation. The four target qualities are calibration, sharpness, focus/locality and propriety. ViEWS 2019/2020: AUROC, AUPR, Brier, separation and model-criticism plots.
unit_of_metric: Pooled: the mean score over all unit-months in a window, per level (cm, pgm), reported per year and as a six-year average. The dashboard offers per-country, per-cell and per-month breakdowns, but the ranking is pooled.
baseline_strength: Strong and decisive. Retrospective 2018-2023 cm averages (CRPS / ab-Log / MIS): exactly_zero 56.84 / 1.59 / 1136.80; last_historical 158.16 / 1.14 / 3137.09 (2023 alone gave CRPS 678.96); conflictology_country12 49.36 / 0.65 / 873.53, the best benchmark; bootstrap240 56.17 / 1.14 / 1101.02. At pgm, exactly_zero and bootstrap240 tie at CRPS 0.45, and neighbors12 is slightly better (0.45 CRPS, MIS 8.61 vs 8.98). True future, Jul 2024 to Jun 2025 (leaderboard, CRPS): at cm the post-hoc benchmark conflictology_country12 ranks 1st with 24.92, ahead of Brandt_NB_GLMM 25.17, Randahl_Vegelius OMM 25.27, ConflictForecast 25.96 and CCEW_tft 26.23. last_historical (26.32) beats 11 of the 17 contributed models. At pgm conflictology_country12 is again 1st (0.27), ahead of the CCEW tree ensembles (0.29) and neighbors12 (0.30). Several complex models score worse than exactly_zero at cm (zero-inflated GAM 61.16, UNITO transformer 64.10), and some Brandt GAMs blew up (CRPS 4.9e5 to 7.8e6). On the secondary metrics, contributions do beat the benchmark: at cm the OMM ab-Log 0.68 beats 0.76 and ConflictForecast MIS 329.7 beats 376.3; at pgm the CCEW trees reach ab-Log 0.09 vs 0.11 and MIS 4.43 vs 4.58. The predecessor competition (Vesco et al. 2022) found the same pattern: most models were beaten by a 'no-change' model. Caveat: the conflictology benchmarks are labelled 'post-hoc' (ph). They were added on scoring-committee advice after the start and are therefore 'not used as scoring rule'. The Drauz & Becker entry used the same logic from the start.
calibration: The challenge itself publishes no reliability diagrams. Calibration is assessed only implicitly, through CRPS and MIS (both reward calibration and sharpness) and through the coverage penalty term of MIS. One contribution (Fritz et al., three-stage hurdle) uses Platt scaling to match the observed relative frequency. ViEWS 2019 calibrated the ensemble so that the mean predicted probability matched the observed frequency (calibration-in-the-large) on the calibration partition, but it separated cases poorly: very few predictions were above 0.75 or below 0.05. ViEWS2020 fitted calibration, EBMA weights and hyper-parameters on the calibration period, then retrained the constituent models on train+calibration before forecasting.
calibration_under_drift: There is no formal test of calibration-in-the-large between validation and test. The paper documents large base-rate swings across windows. Exactly-zero CRPS at cm ranges from 23.02 (2019) to 120.97 (2022) because of the 2021-22 surge (Ethiopia, Ukraine; 2021 was the deadliest year since 1994). last_historical goes from best in 2018-2020 to worst in 2021-2023. The design response is to average over six windows and to add a true-future window, not to recalibrate. ViEWS2020 checked that published true forecasts (Jul 2018 to Dec 2019) scored 'roughly as good as' the earlier out-of-sample evaluation, which is a drift check at the level of AUPR/AUROC. No recalibration method under drift is proposed [uncertain for the planned follow-up evaluation article].
uncertainty_of_gain: Weak. The challenge paper reports no confidence intervals, Diebold-Mariano tests or bootstrap on score differences between models and benchmarks. The true-future ranking at cm separates the top three by less than 1.5% of CRPS (24.92 vs 25.17 vs 25.27), which is almost certainly inside the noise, yet a rank is still assigned. The authors acknowledge that a single year 'will generate a limited amount of data for model evaluation, and the evaluation scores will vary considerably over time'. ViEWS2020 did use a bootstrap standard error of AUPR (resampling forecast-actual pairs) for its 0.5-SE ensemble-pruning rule. That resampling treats unit-months as independent, so it likely understates uncertainty under space-time clustering [uncertain: the exact resampling unit is described in their Online appendix D].
regime_coverage: Good across the conflict regime. The six retrospective years span a low-violence period (2018-2019) and the sharp 2021-2022 escalation (Ethiopia, Ukraine, Yemen), and the score swings make the effect visible. The true future (Jul 2024 to Jun 2025) covers a further real-time regime. None of the Ukrainian alert-specific shifts (Jan-2025 drone surge, Dec-2025 raion reform, Sep-2026 yellow/red) apply. The analogous lesson is that a model ranked on one regime (the 2018-2020 calm) can reverse on the next (last_historical went from best to worst).
leakage_handling: (1) True-future protocol: forecasts for Jul 2024 to Jun 2025 were submitted on 23 Jun 2024, before the outcomes existed, and a preprint was published at the window start as a pre-analysis plan, so neither leakage nor test peeking is possible for that window. (2) Fixed data cut-offs per window: inputs end in October of the prior year (or April 2024), and forecasts start at s=3, which respects the data release lag. This is a label-maturity rule, like our purge rule and D-021's [t-14d, t-H] window. (3) Scoring code and benchmarks are public and fixed in advance (invitation v1.2, Apr 2023), and the organisers compute all scores centrally from submitted samples. MISSED or weak: (a) The retrospective 2018-2023 windows are only pseudo-out-of-sample. Their outcomes (final UCDP-GED) were public, contributors had them during development, and at least one entry (Bodentien & Rueter) tuned its history length 'by minimizing the CRPS in the test set'. Test-window scores can therefore be optimistic, and only the true future is clean. (b) Real-time vintage of external covariates in the retrospective windows is not documented. (c) ViEWS2020 retrains on train+calibration after tuning, so the deployed model differs from the validated one. (d) Benchmarks and the evaluation timeline were changed after the start (post-hoc benchmarks, extended windows).
test_window_hygiene: True future: best practice. It was frozen and submitted before the window, with a public pre-analysis-plan preprint (arXiv 2407.11045, 8 Jul 2024), centrally scored, and continuously monitored on a public dashboard as UCDP Candidate data arrived. An independent scoring committee is planned, weighting test windows and true future roughly equally. Retrospective test windows: poor hygiene, because they were visible and tunable. Contributors received preliminary scores at the October 2023 Berlin workshop and resubmitted final test forecasts in June 2024, so they could iterate on the test windows. Timeline amendments: the invitation (v1.2, 18 Apr 2023) foresaw final submissions on 10 Dec 2023 and a calendar-2024 true future. The actual deadline was 23 Jun 2024 for Jul 2024 to Jun 2025. The 'ph' benchmarks were added later and excluded from the formal ranking for that reason.
headline_results: (1) The simplest strong baseline won the true future. conflictology_country12 (each country's last 12 monthly values used as the forecast distribution) ranks 1st on CRPS at both levels: cm 24.92 vs the best contribution 25.17 (Brandt NB GLMM), and pgm 0.27 vs 0.29 (CCEW trees). As of Feb 2025 PRIO reported that 'Conflictology' led both rankings. (2) On secondary metrics, contributions beat the benchmark: at cm the Randahl-Vegelius OMM has the best ab-Log (0.68) and ConflictForecast the best MIS (329.7); at pgm the CCEW trees reach ab-Log 0.09 and MIS 4.43, vs the benchmark's 0.11 and 4.58. Rankings depend on the metric. (3) last_historical (persistence plus Poisson noise) beat 11 of 17 contributions at cm. Several complex models were worse than predicting zero, and some GAMs diverged catastrophically. (4) Retrospectively (2018-2023), conflictology_country12 is the best benchmark (cm CRPS 49.36). Benchmark scores vary by a factor of about 5 to 30 across years, so a single year is a noisy test. (5) Predecessor competition: most models were beaten by a no-change model. (6) ViEWS2020: the new cm state-based ensemble improved AUPR from 0.838 to 0.864 and Brier from 0.097 to 0.075 on 2016-18, and the published 2018-19 true forecasts performed about as well as the out-of-sample evaluation predicted. The formal evaluation article and the scoring-committee verdict had not been found as of 2026-10-17 [uncertain].
code_available: Yes. https://github.com/prio-data/prediction_competition_2023 holds the benchmark generation and evaluation scripts (CRPS, ab-Log, MIS); there is no license file, and the last push was 2025-12-08. The challenge data, codebook and all submitted forecasts are at https://viewsforecasting.org/research/prediction-challenge-2023/ and https://www.prio.org/jpr/datasets/. The interactive dashboard is at https://predcomp.viewsforecasting.org. The article is CC BY 4.0. The ViEWS production pipeline (views-platform) is open source on GitHub under prio-data/views-platform [uncertain].
takeaways_for_project:
1) Our D-021 choice is directly validated. VIEWS' winning true-future model, conflictology_country12, is literally a rolling recent-history empirical distribution per unit: the cm-level twin of our rolling 14-day recent-rate baseline. A large field of ML, transformer and Bayesian models could not beat it on the primary metric. Treat 'not beating recent-rate' as a likely, legitimate outcome and report it honestly, as CLAUDE.md requires. Also report persistence (raw and calibrated), because last_historical beat most entries.
2) Freeze the baselines before seeing the test. VIEWS had to demote its best benchmark to 'post-hoc, not a scoring rule' because it was added after the start. Our four baselines (climatology, rolling recent-rate with shrinkage (k + 10*p_unit)/(n + 10), raw persistence, calibrated persistence) are fixed in M3 on validation, which is the right call. Do not add or re-specify a baseline after M4 scoring; if one is added, label it post-hoc as VIEWS did.
3) Only a truly unseen window is clean. VIEWS' retrospective windows were visible, and at least one team tuned on them. Our 'score the final test ONCE at end of M4' rule is the equivalent of their true future, and the 2026-07-27 to 09-07 window must never feed tuning. The API new-regime check (D-015) resembles their true-future window most closely, because the model is frozen before that data is scored. Describe it as such, while keeping it exploratory.
4) Label-version shift: VIEWS scores the true future on preliminary UCDP-Candidate data and the test windows on final GED, and flags this as a possible source of systematic differences. This supports D-007/D-015: never mix the official file and alerts.in.ua in one metric, and state that the new-regime numbers use a different label source.
5) Label maturity / purge: VIEWS starts forecasts at s=3 because of the data release lag. Our equivalents are the D-021 [t-14d, t-H] rule and the purge at every cut-off. Keep the truncation/leakage test, with its negative control, as a hard gate.
6) Uncertainty of gain is the gap VIEWS left open. The top three true-future cm models are within 1.5% CRPS, with no CI or significance test, yet they are ranked. Do the D-013 week-block bootstrap CI on the Brier gain over recent-rate (and a DM/HAC test if time allows), keep all 24 units of a block together, and do not claim a winner when the CI covers zero.
7) Persistence credit: VIEWS scores every unit-month, so ongoing wars dominate the scores and persistence wins. Our onset mask (rows already under alert are excluded) and the D-020 24h causal cap remove most of this credit. Do not compare our skill numbers with state-target results from other projects, and cite VIEWS as the example of why state targets inflate skill.
8) Pooled scores can be dominated by a few units (9 of the 10 largest CRPS values came from Ethiopia and Ukraine). Report per group (Kyiv City, frontline, rear), within-oblast mean AUC, and per-oblast reliability (D-013), not only pooled numbers.
9) Single-window volatility: VIEWS benchmark scores swing about 5x across years, and last_historical went from best to worst. Our 6-week test is one short window. Add a per-week breakdown and the optional weekly-refit row (D-014) to show stability, and phrase conclusions as specific to the summer-2026 regime.
10) Metric choice: CRPS for a binary event reduces to the Brier score, so our primary metric (Brier skill score, D-021) is the binary analogue of VIEWS' main metric. Their ab-Log idea (cap the penalty by adding a pseudo-count) mirrors clipping probabilities before computing log loss, if we ever report log loss. Keep PR-AUC / base rate as the secondary 'focus' view, since rankings changed with the metric in VIEWS.
11) Do not refit on train+val after early stopping. ViEWS2020 does this (step 4: retrain on training + calibration), which means the deployed model was never itself validated. Our CLAUDE.md rule (no refit after early stopping; calibration fitted on validation and applied to the same model, D-021) is stricter and should stay.
12) Calibration-in-the-large: ViEWS 2019 calibrated mean predicted to observed frequency but still separated cases poorly. Report both reliability (D-006) and discrimination, and for D-015(c) compare mean predicted vs observed per group in the new regime.
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) A true-future, pre-registered window: freeze the model and baselines, publish or commit the plan before the outcomes exist, and score centrally with fixed code. (b) Fixed proper scoring rules announced up front, with one designated main metric for the ranking (CRPS there, BSS vs recent-rate for us) and secondary metrics for diagnosis. (c) Strong, simple, public benchmarks shipped from day one, especially rolling recent-history and persistence baselines; in VIEWS these were the bar that mattered. (d) Several evaluation windows across regimes, reported per window, plus a six-year average, to expose instability. (e) Fixed data cut-offs that respect publication or label lag (s >= 3 there; purge and [t-14d, t-H] here). (f) Score submissions from full distributions or probabilities, never point forecasts alone, and convert point forecasts explicitly with a documented rule (VIEWS: Poisson). (g) Cap infinite penalties with a pre-specified adjustment (ab-Log pseudo-count) instead of dropping rows. (h) Publish all forecasts, code and data for re-scoring. (i) An independent scoring committee or reviewer (our `reviewer` subagent plays this role). AVOID: (1) Treating historical 'test' windows whose outcomes are public as out-of-sample after teams or authors have tuned on them. (2) Adding benchmarks or changing windows after the start without labelling them post-hoc. (3) Ranking models whose score differences are within noise, without CIs or a DM test. (4) Scoring all unit-periods, including ongoing events, and then presenting the skill as an early-warning (onset) skill. (5) Mixing label versions (preliminary vs final, or official vs API) inside one comparison without flagging it. (6) Retraining on train+validation after tuning, so the deployed model was never validated. (7) Generalising from a single year or regime when benchmark scores swing several-fold between years. (8) Complex models without sanity checks: several GAM/transformer entries were worse than predicting all zeros, and some diverged by 5 orders of magnitude.
